subject: biology
chapter_title: Biomolecules: Chemical Composition of Living Tissues

concepts.title: How to Analyse Chemical Composition of Biomolecules
concepts.definition: Chemical analysis of living tissue involves grinding it in trichloroacetic acid, separating the acid-soluble pool of small molecules from the acid-insoluble fraction of macromolecules, and then identifying the compounds by ash analysis and chromatography techniques.
concepts.key_idea: The acid-soluble pool holds amino acids, sugars and nucleotides, while the insoluble fraction holds proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids, giving the elemental analysis of living tissue.
question_patterns: how is the chemical composition of a tissue analysed
what is the acid soluble pool and what does it contain
distinguish the acid insoluble fraction from the soluble pool
which techniques identify the compounds separated from a tissue
why is trichloroacetic acid used in analysis
state the average elemental composition of living tissue

solution_steps.explain: Recall grinding, acid treatment and filtration of the tissue.
Separate the soluble micromolecules from insoluble macromolecules.
Use chromatography and elemental analysis for identification.

concepts.title: Proteins, Carbohydrates, Lipids and Nucleic Acids
concepts.section: 9.2 Proteins, 9.3 Polysaccharides, 9.4 Nucleic Acids, 9.5 Structure of Proteins
concepts.definition: Biomolecules include carbohydrates as monosaccharides and polysaccharides such as starch, cellulose and glycogen, lipids as fats and phospholipids, proteins as polymers of twenty amino acids showing primary to quaternary structure, and nucleic acids as deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid built of nucleotides.
concepts.key_idea: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, sugars by glycosidic bonds, fatty acids to glycerol by ester bonds, and nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds, forming the giant molecules of life.
question_patterns: classify biomolecules into carbohydrates proteins lipids and nucleic acids
describe the primary secondary tertiary and quaternary structure of proteins
what are zwitter ions in amino acids
differentiate DNA and RNA as nucleic acids
name the bonds joining monomers in each biomolecule
explain the structure of starch cellulose and glycogen

solution_steps.explain: Note whether the molecule is built of sugars, amino acids, nucleotides or fatty acids.
Match the bond type to the biomolecule class.
Assign storage, structural, enzymatic or hereditary role.

concepts.title: Enzymes: Nature, Classes and Factors Affecting Activity
concepts.definition: Enzymes are proteinaceous biocatalysts that lower activation energy and act on a substrate through an active site; they are classified into six classes of oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases, and their activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration, and is checked by competitive inhibition.
concepts.key_idea: At optimum temperature and pH the enzyme velocity rises with substrate concentration until all active sites are occupied, and a competitive inhibitor mimics the substrate at the active site.
question_patterns: define enzymes and explain how they lower activation energy
name the six classes of enzymes with examples
how do temperature and ph affect enzyme activity
what is competitive inhibition of an enzyme
explain the role of the active site and substrate in catalysis
what are coenzymes and prosthetic groups

solution_steps.explain: Read the reaction type to place the enzyme in one of the six classes.
Note the temperature, pH and substrate concentration of the reaction.
Predict whether activity rises, falls or is inhibited.

concepts.title: Metabolism and the Living State of Cells
concepts.definition: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the living cell, made of anabolic pathways that build complex molecules from simpler ones with energy consumption and catabolic pathways that break down molecules releasing energy, with ATP as the energy currency.
concepts.key_idea: The living state is a non-equilibrium steady state that continuously exchanges energy and matter, and metabolism provides the flow of energy through anabolic and catabolic reactions.
question_patterns: define metabolism and its two phases
differentiate anabolic and catabolic pathways with examples
why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell
what is meant by the living state being a non-equilibrium steady state
give examples of metabolic reactions in the cell
how do catabolic reactions release energy

solution_steps.explain: Place each reaction in anabolism or catabolism.
Note whether energy is consumed or released as ATP.
Link the pathways to the steady non-equilibrium state of the cell.
